title: September 2019 Class College Final Exam (Part 1 of 6)
unit: Comprehensive Nursing (Medical-Surgical, Paediatrics, Midwifery, Community Health, Mental Health, Pharmacology, Research, Leadership and Management)

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the September 2019 class College Final Exam paper (Kenya Registered Nursing, sat 18 November 2022, Multiple Choice Questions, Q1 to Q20).

questions.text: The eye structure that regulates the intensity of light reaching the retina is:
questions.explanation: Iris (B) is correct because it is the pigmented muscular diaphragm around the pupil. Its circular sphincter muscle constricts the pupil in bright light and its radial dilator muscle enlarges the pupil in dim light, so it controls how much light enters the eye. Cornea (A) is incorrect because it is the transparent front layer that does most of the light bending (refraction) but does not adjust the amount of light. Lens (C) is incorrect because it changes shape (accommodation) to focus light on the retina. Vitreous body (D) is incorrect because it is the clear gel in the posterior segment that maintains the shape of the eyeball and transmits light to the retina.

questions.text: The following are risk factors of cataracts:
questions.explanation: Use of steroids, family history (A) is the marked answer because long-term corticosteroid use (oral, inhaled or topical) causes posterior subcapsular lens opacities, and a family history increases the chance of earlier or inherited cataract. Other recognised risks are diabetes mellitus, smoking, excessive ultraviolet exposure and alcohol. Trauma, aging (B) lists factors that also contribute (injury to the lens and age-related protein changes), so this item is contestable, but the key given on the paper is A. Poor hygiene, bacterial conjunctivitis (C) is incorrect because conjunctival infections affect the conjunctiva and do not opacify the lens. Viral conjunctivitis, trauma (D) is incorrect because the conjunctivitis part is not a cataract risk factor.

questions.text: A priority intervention for a child diagnosed with pyloric stenosis is:
questions.explanation: Withholding oral feeds (B) is correct because the infant has projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds and is dehydrated with hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Feeds are stopped (nil by mouth) and IV fluids with electrolytes are given to correct this before surgery (pyloromyotomy). Administration of laxative (A) is incorrect because the obstruction is at the pylorus and a laxative would only worsen fluid loss. Feeding via nasogastric tube (C) is incorrect because feeding into an obstructed stomach increases vomiting and the risk of aspiration (an NG tube is used only to decompress the stomach). Warm compresses over the abdomen (D) is incorrect because they cannot relieve the hypertrophied pyloric muscle, which is cured only by surgery.

questions.text: In Gastroschisis:

options.A: The bowels are pushed into the inguinal ring
options.B: Large intestines invaginates into its proximal part
options.C: Bowels protrude through the abdominal wall

questions.explanation: Bowels protrude through the abdominal wall (C) is correct because gastroschisis is a congenital defect of the anterior abdominal wall, usually to the right of the umbilicus, through which loops of bowel herniate with no covering sac (in omphalocele there is a sac). Nursing care includes covering the exposed bowel with warm saline-soaked sterile gauze or plastic wrap, keeping the baby warm, passing an NG tube and giving IV fluids before surgical repair. The bowels are pushed into the inguinal ring (A) is incorrect because it describes an inguinal hernia. Large intestines invaginates into its proximal part (B) is incorrect because it describes intussusception. Peristaltic movement ceases (D) is incorrect because it describes paralytic ileus, not the defining feature of gastroschisis.

questions.text: Estimated replacement fluid volume for a child weighing 14kgs with 25% burns is:
questions.explanation: 1400mls (B) is correct using the Parkland formula: 4 ml x body weight (14 kg) x percentage burn (25) = 1400 ml in the first 24 hours, with half (700 ml) given in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn and the other half over the next 16 hours. In children, maintenance fluids are added on top of this in practice. 2500mls (A) is incorrect because it overestimates the requirement and does not come from the formula. 1000mls (C) is incorrect because it is about 2.9 ml/kg/% burn, below the 3 to 4 ml/kg/% used. 500mls (D) is incorrect because it is far too little and would leave the child in burn shock.

questions.text: A child brought to the accident and emergency with complaints of diarrhea with blood is suspected to have:
questions.explanation: Dysentery (B) is correct because in the IMCI classification, diarrhoea with visible blood in the stool is dysentery, most commonly caused by Shigella, and it is treated with an oral antibiotic (ciprofloxacin) plus ORS and zinc. Cholera (A) is incorrect because it causes profuse watery 'rice water' stools without blood. Amoebiasis (C) is incorrect as the best answer because, although Entamoeba histolytica can cause bloody diarrhoea, it is less common in young children and is considered when bloody diarrhoea persists after treatment for Shigella. Gastritis (D) is incorrect because it is inflammation of the stomach lining causing epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, not bloody diarrhoea.

questions.text: A priority intervention for a child who is convulsing now is:
questions.explanation: Keeping in recovery position (A) is correct because the first priority in a convulsing child is to protect the airway, prevent aspiration and avoid injury: place the child in the recovery (lateral) position, loosen tight clothing, clear the surroundings, note the time, give oxygen and then give an anticonvulsant such as rectal or IV diazepam and check blood glucose. Restraining their limbs (B) is incorrect because it can cause fractures and muscle injury and does not stop the seizure. Establishing IV access (C) is incorrect as the first step because it is done after the airway is protected and is difficult during active convulsions. Inserting an oropharyngeal airway (D) is incorrect because forcing a device into a clenched jaw can injure the teeth and soft tissues and provoke vomiting.

questions.text: Non probability sampling designs:

options.A: Allow generalization of research findings to the target population
options.C: Are used when the population has well defined sampling frame
options.D: Are ideal for experimental type of research

questions.explanation: Include quota sampling and snowballing (B) is correct because in non-probability sampling not every element has a known chance of selection, and the types include convenience, quota, purposive (judgemental), snowball (network) and consecutive sampling. Allow generalization of research findings to the target population (A) is incorrect because generalisation needs probability (random) sampling. Are used when the population has well defined sampling frame (C) is incorrect because probability sampling needs a well-defined sampling frame; non-probability methods are used when no frame is available. Are ideal for experimental type of research (D) is incorrect because experimental studies rely on random sampling and random assignment to reduce bias.

questions.text: In research, the ethical principle of beneficence refers to:
questions.explanation: Doing good (D) is correct because beneficence means that the researcher must maximise benefits and minimise harm, protecting participants from physical and psychological harm and from exploitation, and weighing the risk-benefit ratio of the study. Right to self determination (A) is incorrect because it describes autonomy (respect for persons), where participants decide freely whether to take part or withdraw. Confidentiality (B) is incorrect because it is the protection of the information participants give so that it is not disclosed or traced to them. Right to privacy (C) is incorrect because it is the right to control when and how much personal information is shared.

questions.text: In severe acute malnutrition, the most common features of severe infection are:

options.D: Increased white cell count, reduced erythrocyte count

questions.explanation: Hypothermia, hypoglycemia (B) is correct because malnourished children have a weak immune response, so the usual signs of infection such as fever and a raised white cell count are often absent, and severe infection shows as hypothermia and hypoglycaemia. This is why every child admitted with severe acute malnutrition is given broad-spectrum antibiotics, kept warm and fed or given 10% glucose early. Fever, Increased ESR (A) is incorrect because fever is often absent and ESR is not a bedside sign. Hyperglycemia, Fever (C) is incorrect because severe malnutrition predisposes to low, not high, blood glucose. Increased white cell count, reduced erythrocyte count (D) is incorrect because the white count is frequently normal or low, and anaemia is common but is not a sign of infection.

questions.text: Nursing consideration for a child suffering from Laryngo-tracheobronchitis include:
questions.explanation: Steam inhalation (C) is the marked answer because in croup (usually parainfluenza virus) with barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor, the nursing care taught is to keep the child calm and upright, give humidified or cool mist to soothe the inflamed larynx and loosen secretions, encourage oral fluids and monitor respiratory rate, stridor and retractions (note: mist has limited proven benefit, and steam carries a scald risk). Dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline are used for moderate to severe croup. Isolation for 7 days (A) is incorrect because droplet precautions apply only while symptomatic. Monitoring for chest tube drainage (B) is incorrect because it belongs to pleural effusion or pneumothorax care. Immunization with flu vaccine (D) is incorrect because it is prevention, not nursing care of the acute illness.

questions.text: Management of functional incontinence due to cognitive impairment includes:
questions.explanation: Prompted voiding (D) is correct because functional incontinence occurs when the urinary tract is intact but cognitive or physical impairment (for example dementia) prevents the person from recognising the need to void or reaching the toilet. Care involves regular reminders and prompts, scheduled toileting, easy access to the toilet and simple clothing. Bladder training (A) is incorrect because it needs intact cognition and is used mainly for urge incontinence. Urethral catheterization (B) is incorrect because it is reserved for retention or as a last resort because of infection risk. Pelvic floor exercises (C) is incorrect because they treat stress incontinence and need the ability to follow instructions.

questions.text: Clinical findings in a child with nephrotic syndrome include:
questions.explanation: Proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, edema (B) is correct because damage to the glomerular basement membrane leaks large amounts of protein into the urine, the serum albumin falls, the low oncotic pressure lets fluid move into tissues (periorbital oedema, ascites, scrotal oedema), and the liver produces more lipoproteins so cholesterol and triglycerides rise. Proteinuria, hyperalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, edema (A) is incorrect because albumin is low, not high. Proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hypolipidemia, edema (C) is incorrect because blood lipids are raised, not low. Proteinuria, hyperalbuminemia, hypolipidemia, edema (D) is incorrect because it gets both the albumin and the lipid changes the wrong way round.

questions.text: Management of a patient with calcium urolithiasis includes:
questions.explanation: Increased fluid intake (A) is correct because a high fluid intake (about 2.5 to 3 litres a day, enough for urine output above 2 litres) dilutes the urine and lowers the concentration of calcium salts, which reduces stone formation and helps passage of small stones. Other measures are a low sodium, moderate calcium diet, thiazide diuretics and pain relief. Administration of sodium bicarbonate (B) is incorrect because alkalinising the urine is used for uric acid and cystine stones, and calcium phosphate stones form in alkaline urine. Administer allopurinol (C) is incorrect because it lowers uric acid and is used for uric acid stones and gout. Encouraging a low purine diet (D) is incorrect because it applies to uric acid stones.

questions.text: A client using the following method of family planning is at a higher risk of developing fractures due to osteoporosis:
questions.explanation: Depo provera (C) is correct because depot medroxyprogesterone acetate suppresses ovarian oestrogen production, and long-term use reduces bone mineral density, so users are counselled on calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise. Microlut pills (A) is incorrect because it is a progestogen-only pill (levonorgestrel) that does not significantly suppress oestrogen or lower bone density. Norigynon (B) is incorrect because it is a monthly combined injectable (norethisterone enanthate with estradiol valerate) containing oestrogen, so bone density is preserved. Microgynon pills (D) is incorrect because it is a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol.

questions.text: A client reports to the FP clinic with complaints of blurred vision, severe calf pains and chest pains. The nurse suspects that the client has been using the following method of family planning:
questions.explanation: Combined oral contraceptive pill (D) is correct because the oestrogen in the pill increases clotting factors and the risk of thromboembolism: severe calf pain suggests deep vein thrombosis, chest pain suggests pulmonary embolism, and blurred vision suggests retinal vessel thrombosis or hypertension. These are danger signs, so the pill is stopped and the client is referred urgently. Progesterone releasing vaginal ring (A) is incorrect because it releases a progestogen and is not linked to this picture. Copper based intrauterine contraceptive device (B) is incorrect because it is hormone free and its problems are heavier periods, cramps and pelvic infection. Progesterone injectable (C) is incorrect because its usual effects are menstrual changes, weight gain and delayed return of fertility.

questions.text: In Medical Eligibility Criteria for contraceptive use if a client has a condition in category 3, the nurse understands that:

options.A: Use of the method requires extreme care
options.B: The method should not be used
options.C: There is no restriction on use of the method
options.D: Close follow up is needed for the client

questions.explanation: Use of the method requires extreme care (A) is the marked answer because category 3 means the theoretical or proven risks usually outweigh the advantages, so the method is not usually recommended unless other more appropriate methods are unavailable or unacceptable, and if it is used it needs careful clinical judgement and close monitoring. The method should not be used (B) is incorrect because it describes category 4 (unacceptable health risk). There is no restriction on use of the method (C) is incorrect because it describes category 1. Close follow up is needed for the client (D) is incorrect as the best answer because it reflects the lighter caution of category 2 (can generally use, some follow-up may be needed).

questions.text: A preoperative patient receives atropine before induction of anaesthesia. The nurse caring for this patient understands that this agent is used to prevent:
questions.explanation: Gastric secretions (D) is the marked answer because atropine is an anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) premedication that dries salivary, bronchial and, to a lesser extent, gastric secretions, lowering the risk of aspiration and laryngospasm, and it also blocks vagal reflex bradycardia during intubation. Anxiety (A) is incorrect because it is prevented by anxiolytics such as diazepam or midazolam. Tachycardia (B) is incorrect because atropine causes tachycardia; it is used to prevent bradycardia. Hypertension (C) is incorrect because atropine has no role in preventing high blood pressure.

questions.text: Mr. X is on diazepam for anxiety management. He takes an overdose, the drug of choice in his management is:
questions.explanation: Flumazenil (B) is correct because it is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor and reverses sedation and respiratory depression from diazepam. It is given slowly IV with airway support, and the nurse watches for seizures in dependent patients and for re-sedation, since its action is shorter than that of diazepam. Naloxone (A) is incorrect because it reverses opioids. Epinephrine (C) is incorrect because it is used for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest. Neostigmine (D) is incorrect because it is a cholinesterase inhibitor used to reverse non-depolarising muscle relaxants and to treat myasthenia gravis.

questions.text: The nurse will monitor for the following side effects in a patient on dexamethasone:
questions.explanation: Hyperglycemia (B) is correct because corticosteroids increase gluconeogenesis and cause insulin resistance, so blood glucose rises (steroid-induced diabetes); other effects to monitor are fluid and sodium retention, hypertension, hypokalaemia, peptic ulcers, infection risk, osteoporosis and mood changes. Dehydration (A) is incorrect because steroids cause sodium and water retention. Hypotension (C) is incorrect because steroids tend to raise blood pressure; hypotension appears with adrenal insufficiency after abrupt withdrawal. Hypothermia (D) is incorrect because steroids suppress the immune response and can mask fever, but they do not cause hypothermia.
